title: Ganesh Kumar vs Babita Aggarwal on 21 May, 2026
full_text: Ganesh Kumar vs Babita Aggarwal on 21 May, 2026 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal CC No. 580/2019 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CNR number DLSE020015122019 2. Name of the complainant Sh. Ganesh Kumar, S/o Sh. Ram Lal Varshney, R/o H. No. G- 156-A, 3rd Floor, Gali NO. 10, Mohan Baba Nagar, Near Canara Bank ATM, Badarpur, New Delhi - 110044. 3. Name of the accused person(s), parentage Mrs. Babita Aggarwal, & residential address W/o Sh. Vinod Kumar, R/o H. No. G-156-A, Ground Floor, Gali No. CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 1 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.21 16:51:34 +0530 10, Mohan Baba Nagar, Near Canara Bank ATM, Badarpur, New Delhi - 110044. 4. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Convicted 7. Date of judgment/order 21.05.2026 Date of Institution : 18.01.2019 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 11.05.2026 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 21.05.2026 ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Mr. Abhay Bhati Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Mr. Shubham Gupta JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Sh. Ganesh Kumar (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 2 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.21 16:51:42 +0530 Ms. Babita Aggarwal under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant and the accused had friendly relations with each other as they were neighbours. That, the accused approached the complainant on 09.03.2014 for a friendly loan of Rs. 2,00,000/- to meet some of his urgent requirement and the accused promised to return the loan amount within 2 years. That, the complainant and the accused also executed an agreement to assure the complainant. That, as per the instance of the accused, on 10.03.2014, the amount of Rs. 2,00,000/- was transferred in the bank account of the son of the accused by the complainant as a friendly loan. That, the accused had issued three post dated cheques in favour of the complainant to discharge her legal liability, i.e., bearing no. 698458 dated 04.12.2018 amounting to Rs. 50,000/-, bearing no. 698459 dated 04.12.2018 amounting to Rs. 75,000/- and bearing no. 698460 dated 04.12.2018 amounting to Rs. 75,000/-, all drawn on State Bank of India, Ambedkar Nagar, Sector V, Dakshin Puri, New Delhi. That, the complainant asked the accused to repay the liability, however the accused sought more time due to financial difficulty. That, in November 2018, the accused assured the complainant that the cheques in question shall be honoured upon presentation. That, believing the assurances and representation of the accused, the complainant presented the abovesaid cheques with his banker ICICI Bank Ltd., Mohan Cooperative Industrial Area, Mathura Road, New Delhi, however CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 3 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.21 16:51:48 +0530 the said cheques were dishonoured with the remarks "Stop Payment" vide return memos dated 07.12.2018. B. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 21.12.2018, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/1 and relied on documents Ex. CW1/A to Ex. CW1/K. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused person, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon them to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has admitted her signatures on the cheque in question and has admitted to receiving the legal demand notice. The accused has stated that she took a loan in the sum of Rs. 2 lakhs from the complainant and the cheques in question were issued in favour of the complainant at that time. The accused has further stated that the complainant bought the 3rd floor of CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 4 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:51:55 +0530 the house of the accused and deducted the loan amount of Rs. 2 lakhs from the payment of the third floor and the accused owes no liability towards the complainant. 6. Vide separate statement of accused, admissions and denial u/s 294 CrPC was done and witness no. 2 and 3 were dropped from the list of complainant witnesses. 7. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 16.09.2023. Accordingly, the matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused person. 8. Statement of accused person under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 03.01.2024 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. DW-1 was examined in chief, cross-examined and discharged. DE was closed vide order of this court by recording a statement of the accused on 25.02.2026. 9. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 10. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 5 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:00 +0530 RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 11. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 6 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:06 +0530 II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 12. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheques, i.e., bearing no. 698458 dated 04.12.2018 for Rs. 50,000/-, bearing no. 698459 dated 04.12.2018 for Rs. 75,000/- and bearing no. 698460 dated 04.12.2018 in the sum of Rs. 75,000/-, all drawn on State Bank of India, Dakshinpuri, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/B, Ex. CW1/C & Ex. CW1/D). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 7 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:14 +0530 admitted that the cheques in dispute belong to her. It is also not disputed that the cheques in question are not drawn on the account maintained by the accused and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheques. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 13. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheques in question were returned vide return memos dated 07.12.2018 (Ex. CW1/E, Ex. CW1/F & Ex. CW1/G) due to the reason "Stop Payment." By implication thereof, the cheques were presented within three months and the same were returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 14. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 21.12.2018 (Ex. CW1/H) was dispatched on 22.12.2018 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/I), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has admitted to receiving of the legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. Furthermore, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 8 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:19 +0530 virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 15. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 16. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 9 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:24 +0530 his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 17. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 18. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 19. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/1 and the loan agreement executed between the CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 10 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:28 +0530 complainant and the accused Ex. CW1/A. The case of the complainant is that the accused had issued the cheque in question in discharge of her liability qua the loan taken from the complainant. The accused has admitted the loan but has stated that the same was adjusted against the purchase of a property of the accused by the complainant. 20. The accused has argued that the agreement nowhere mentions that the amount of Rs. 2 lakhs were transferred in the account of the son of the accused or that the witnesses to the agreement in question were never examined. However, the accused in her notice u/s 251 CrPC has admitted to having taken a loan of Rs. 2 lakh from the complainant. Further, the accused in her statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC has contradicted herself by stating that the loan was advanced by the complainant to the son of the accused, however she has admitted to being the guarantor for the said loan and issuing the cheques in question qua the said loan. Furthermore, the accused as DW-1 has stated that the said loan amount was adjusted by the complainant in the purchase of the third floor of the accused by the complainant. Therefore, the accused has impliedly admitted the loan agreement and the liability qua the same. 21. A bare perusal of agreement Ex. CW1/A reveals that the loan of Rs. 2 lakhs was to be paid within 2 years and the same was to be repaid by the accused in 24 installments of Rs. 9700/- each. The accused has argued that the amount of loan advanced by the complainant was less than Rs. 2 lakhs, however the accused has not placed any statement of account on record to indicate the amount transferred by the complainant in the account of the son of the accused. It is an established rule of law that under Section 91 and 92 of Indian Evidence Act, no oral evidence can be given qua variation, subtraction, addition or CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 11 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:33 +0530 contradiction of any term of any contract, grant or disposition which is reduced into a document and only documentary evidence or secondary evidence of its contents are admissible. In the present case, the agreement Ex. CW1/1 mentions that the loan was in the sum of Rs. 2 lakhs and unless any documentary evidence is placed on record to contradict the same, the contents of Ex. CW1/1 are only admissible. 22. Furthermore, the agreement Ex. CW1/1 states that the accused was to repay the loan in 24 installments of Rs. 9700/- each, thereby taking the amount to Rs. 2,32,800/- owed by the accused to the complainant. In the present case, the cheque in question is of Rs. 2,00,000/-. Therefore the argument of the accused that the liability owed by the accused is not as much as is stated by the complainant in his cheque in question does not hold any ground. 23. The accused has further argued that the loan amount of Rs. 2 lakh was deemed to be adjusted with the complainant as the complainant had purchased the third floor of the property of the accused vide Ex. DW1/1 and the consideration value of the property in question was Rs. 13 lakh, however the complainant adjusted the loan and the interest amount and the property was sold by the accused for Rs. 8 lakhs. A bare perusal of the sale agreement Ex. DW1/1 indicates that the consideration amount for the property in question is stated as Rs. 8 lakhs and the accused has not placed any document on record to prove that the consideration amount was Rs. 13 lakhs and not Rs. 8 lakhs. The contents of Ex. DW1/1 shall be admissible as is, in light of the discussion u/s 91 and 92 of Indian Evidence Act. 24. In the present case, the accused has failed to even create any doubt, let alone discharging his burden of proof to rebut the presumption u/s 138 , NI Act. The accused has neither brought any witness nor any documentary evidence on record to CC No. 580/2019 Ganesh Kumar Vs. Babita Agarwal Page 12 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.21 16:52:38 +0530 substantiate his claim. It is the duty of the accused to punch holes in the story of the complainant which he has not been able to do. On the other hand, the complainant has brought documentary evidence to prove his version of the story alongwith the benefit of presumption u/s 139 , NI Act in his favour. 25. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 26. Accordingly, Accused Babita Agarwal is held guilty and is convicted of the offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. 27. Copy of this judgment be given to the convict free of cost as per rules. PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA TODAY ON 21st May, 2026.
